## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai Shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.
- Domains: generate-domain-names checks whether a name or domain idea is available and what it costs to register, and suggests available alternatives.

Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.

3	Why (30 real practice runs): suppliers answer visible moves with moves and send `final_offer` when

10	  must-haves, beats the case alternative and is no worse than the thread's opening quote; accept it
11	  when the supplier says final_offer/agreed, or met our last price, or repeated itself (after >= 3 of
12	  our messages), or it is our last allowed message.

14	  price when they ask for more), then every round close 25% (rising by 5 points a round, cap 50%) of the
15	  gap to their best standing price, at least 1% of price (while they move: at most 0.25 x their last

108:### What replicates, what is contested, and what is untested
112:**Hard versus soft bargaining trades money against relationship, and our AI-versus-human result agrees.** Hüffmeier et al. 2014 is a meta-analysis of 34 studies of distributive negotiation (not of training, which one note wrongly claimed): hardline strategies gave better economic outcomes and softline better socioemotional ones, with softliners doing best when they reciprocated concessions accurately ([UvA](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812)). Herold et al. 2025 shows the same split with a chatbot buyer: the competitive prompt won larger discounts in all three studies, near 10 percent with students but only about 1-5.5 percent with professional negotiators, while the collaborative prompt earned more supplier trust, satisfaction and willingness to deal again ([Herold et al., read in full](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214)). The authors flag that the competitive prompts included threats, so "competitive" is confounded with threats, and that the model tended to concede under pushback. We should assume Tacto's bots resemble the professionals, not the students.
114:**Emotion is the most context-dependent area.** Anger drew bigger concessions than happiness in Van Kleef, De Dreu and Manstead 2004 and in a Dutch direct replication ([Pollmann 2017](https://research.tilburguniversity.edu/en/publications/boosheid-en-blijdschap-in-onderhandelingen-een-replicatie-van-van/)), but a Many Labs 5 replication of a related design found an effect about one ninth of the original ([Skorb et al. 2020](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/ampps/2515245920927643/)), and the effect depends on power, intensity, sincerity and the expresser. Anger also invited covert retaliation ([Wang, Northcraft, Van Kleef 2012](https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/publications/beyond-negotiated-outcomes-the-hidden-costs-of-anger-expression-i/)). The review by Van Kleef and Côté is narrative, and the notes found no meta-analysis of anger in negotiation. Gratitude inviting tougher counteroffers rests on one summarised paper with unverified authorship. We therefore label emotion-as-tactic moderate to weak and keep the "no threats, polite" rule on the safer side.
118:### Procurement evidence is thinner than the bargaining evidence
120:Kelly and Chicksand 2024 reviewed 427 papers and found that practitioners mix distributive and integrative moves, a firm stance is often needed at the end, informed buyers pay less, bargaining power comes from spend volume, bundling and alternatives, and fewer than 13 percent of papers use a theory ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9)). The Kraljic matrix is a heuristic more than a law. Kang et al. 2018 found with 77 sourcing professionals that effective buyers chose competitive, collaborative or accommodative styles by quadrant ([Emerald](https://www.emeraldinsight.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/MD-09-2016-0662/full/html)), yet a survey of 107 sourcing projects found the full range of levers used in all four quadrants ([Hesping and Schiele](https://research.utwente.nl/en/publications/matching-tactical-sourcing-levers-with-the-kralji%C4%8D-matrix-empiric/)), and an interview study found hard bargaining present even in strategic relationships ([Lambrechts et al., IPSERA](https://research.ou.nl/en/publications/how-do-buyers-actually-negotiate-with-their-leverage-and-strategi/)). Power research says coercive and mediated power lowers relationship quality ([Leonidou et al. meta-analysis of 120 studies, abstract](https://www.springerprofessional.de/a-meta-analysis-of-power-in-buyer-seller-relationships-an-abstra/16589268)), and reverse auctions cut price while eroding cooperation ([Fugger et al. 2019](https://personal.utdallas.edu/~ekatok/trust-procurement-interactions.pdf)). The Princeton chapter adds that relationships matter economically mostly where value is created after signing (services), much less for plain goods purchases, which matters because Tacto bots remember only within a case. Payment-term and index-clause material came only from vendor blogs and is low quality; no peer-reviewed source was found for should-cost, dual sourcing or supplier development.
122:### AI and LLM negotiation experiments (lower confidence, read last)
126:The pattern most relevant to us is that accommodating buyers lose. In 15,000 negotiations among five frontier models, the buyer with the highest concession rate and fewest rounds had the worst buyer surplus share (24.3 percent) and deal rate (86.4 percent), while winners anchored aggressively and stayed patient ([Li, Bergemann et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16472), partial read). LLMs anchor and split the difference: final prices correlated 0.716 with the initial proposal in one GPT-4 game ([Bianchi et al., NegotiationArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05863), partial read), and buyers were weaker than sellers across 14 models, with a deterministic offer generator (LLM writes only the wording) lifting the buyer deal rate from 26.67 percent to 88.88 percent on 2023-era models against an LLM seller ([Xia et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15813), partial read). Scaffolding helped mid-tier models but not the top ones, and arithmetic accuracy jumped by model generation (GPT-4.1 5.4 percent against GPT-5.2 100 percent) ([PieArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05302), partial read). The only large warmth result is AI-to-AI: warm prompts did better across 180,000+ negotiations, dominance claimed more value in closed deals, and long conversations went with impasse ([Vaccaro et al., PNAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06416), partial read; one model, GPT-4o-mini). That conflicts in emphasis with Herold's human-supplier result, which is why the human-evidence rule 8 stays "firm numbers, polite tone". Human-AI studies are thin: fairness and trust dropped when an AI partner was disclosed (N = 3,552, [preprint abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12773)), and prompt injection that works on AI counterparts does not work on humans, so the threat depends on whether the Tacto supplier is an LLM or a script, which we do not know. One preprint claims negotiation ability does not improve with better models, while PieArena shows large generational gains; the notes attribute this to different metrics and leave it unresolved. The supportive design implication is modest: let the LLM write and let code decide limits, arithmetic and concession schedule, as in the Cicero precedent that the notes describe from memory only.

108:### What replicates, what is contested, and what is untested
112:**Hard versus soft bargaining trades money against relationship, and our AI-versus-human result agrees.** Hüffmeier et al. 2014 is a meta-analysis of 34 studies of distributive negotiation (not of training, which one note wrongly claimed): hardline strategies gave better economic outcomes and softline better socioemotional ones, with softliners doing best when they reciprocated concessions accurately ([UvA](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812)). Herold et al. 2025 shows the same split with a chatbot buyer: the competitive prompt won larger discounts in all three studies, near 10 percent with students but only about 1-5.5 percent with professional negotiators, while the collaborative prompt earned more supplier trust, satisfaction and willingness to deal again ([Herold et al., read in full](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214)). The authors flag that the competitive prompts included threats, so "competitive" is confounded with threats, and that the model tended to concede under pushback. We should assume Tacto's bots resemble the professionals, not the students.
114:**Emotion is the most context-dependent area.** Anger drew bigger concessions than happiness in Van Kleef, De Dreu and Manstead 2004 and in a Dutch direct replication ([Pollmann 2017](https://research.tilburguniversity.edu/en/publications/boosheid-en-blijdschap-in-onderhandelingen-een-replicatie-van-van/)), but a Many Labs 5 replication of a related design found an effect about one ninth of the original ([Skorb et al. 2020](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/ampps/2515245920927643/)), and the effect depends on power, intensity, sincerity and the expresser. Anger also invited covert retaliation ([Wang, Northcraft, Van Kleef 2012](https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/publications/beyond-negotiated-outcomes-the-hidden-costs-of-anger-expression-i/)). The review by Van Kleef and Côté is narrative, and the notes found no meta-analysis of anger in negotiation. Gratitude inviting tougher counteroffers rests on one summarised paper with unverified authorship. We therefore label emotion-as-tactic moderate to weak and keep the "no threats, polite" rule on the safer side.
118:### Procurement evidence is thinner than the bargaining evidence
120:Kelly and Chicksand 2024 reviewed 427 papers and found that practitioners mix distributive and integrative moves, a firm stance is often needed at the end, informed buyers pay less, bargaining power comes from spend volume, bundling and alternatives, and fewer than 13 percent of papers use a theory ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9)). The Kraljic matrix is a heuristic more than a law. Kang et al. 2018 found with 77 sourcing professionals that effective buyers chose competitive, collaborative or accommodative styles by quadrant ([Emerald](https://www.emeraldinsight.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/MD-09-2016-0662/full/html)), yet a survey of 107 sourcing projects found the full range of levers used in all four quadrants ([Hesping and Schiele](https://research.utwente.nl/en/publications/matching-tactical-sourcing-levers-with-the-kralji%C4%8D-matrix-empiric/)), and an interview study found hard bargaining present even in strategic relationships ([Lambrechts et al., IPSERA](https://research.ou.nl/en/publications/how-do-buyers-actually-negotiate-with-their-leverage-and-strategi/)). Power research says coercive and mediated power lowers relationship quality ([Leonidou et al. meta-analysis of 120 studies, abstract](https://www.springerprofessional.de/a-meta-analysis-of-power-in-buyer-seller-relationships-an-abstra/16589268)), and reverse auctions cut price while eroding cooperation ([Fugger et al. 2019](https://personal.utdallas.edu/~ekatok/trust-procurement-interactions.pdf)). The Princeton chapter adds that relationships matter economically mostly where value is created after signing (services), much less for plain goods purchases, which matters because Tacto bots remember only within a case. Payment-term and index-clause material came only from vendor blogs and is low quality; no peer-reviewed source was found for should-cost, dual sourcing or supplier development.
122:### AI and LLM negotiation experiments (lower confidence, read last)
126:The pattern most relevant to us is that accommodating buyers lose. In 15,000 negotiations among five frontier models, the buyer with the highest concession rate and fewest rounds had the worst buyer surplus share (24.3 percent) and deal rate (86.4 percent), while winners anchored aggressively and stayed patient ([Li, Bergemann et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16472), partial read). LLMs anchor and split the difference: final prices correlated 0.716 with the initial proposal in one GPT-4 game ([Bianchi et al., NegotiationArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05863), partial read), and buyers were weaker than sellers across 14 models, with a deterministic offer generator (LLM writes only the wording) lifting the buyer deal rate from 26.67 percent to 88.88 percent on 2023-era models against an LLM seller ([Xia et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15813), partial read). Scaffolding helped mid-tier models but not the top ones, and arithmetic accuracy jumped by model generation (GPT-4.1 5.4 percent against GPT-5.2 100 percent) ([PieArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05302), partial read). The only large warmth result is AI-to-AI: warm prompts did better across 180,000+ negotiations, dominance claimed more value in closed deals, and long conversations went with impasse ([Vaccaro et al., PNAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06416), partial read; one model, GPT-4o-mini). That conflicts in emphasis with Herold's human-supplier result, which is why the human-evidence rule 8 stays "firm numbers, polite tone". Human-AI studies are thin: fairness and trust dropped when an AI partner was disclosed (N = 3,552, [preprint abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12773)), and prompt injection that works on AI counterparts does not work on humans, so the threat depends on whether the Tacto supplier is an LLM or a script, which we do not know. One preprint claims negotiation ability does not improve with better models, while PieArena shows large generational gains; the notes attribute this to different metrics and leave it unresolved. The supportive design implication is modest: let the LLM write and let code decide limits, arithmetic and concession schedule, as in the Cicero precedent that the notes describe from memory only.

def _units_before(case, t, years):
    """Units bought between the horizon start and the date a new price takes effect."""
    start = horizon_start(case)
    if not t.get("effective_date") or start is None:
        return 0.0
    lag = (date.fromisoformat(t["effective_date"]) - start).days / 365
    return t["volume_per_year"] * min(max(lag, 0.0), years)


def supplier_value(case, terms, supplier):
    """What a deal is worth to the supplier per unit, in cash: the price at its standard terms that
    would pay it the same. `supplier` is your estimate of it:
      standard       its standard terms (quote PDF, `docs.standard_terms`)
      interest_rate  what money now is worth to it per year (more to a supplier short of cash)
      usual_rate     its usual cost of money (default: interest_rate); tooling paid up front is
                     worth more to it when cash is dearer than usual
      ppm            the defect rate it really achieves (default: its standard ppm commitment)
      extra          EUR per unit it gains (+) or spends (-) beyond these items, e.g. overtime for
                     a faster delivery or idle capacity a larger volume fills (default 0)
    Contract length and an index clause are security, not cash: they do not count here."""
    b, std = case["buyer"], {**supplier["standard"], **case.get("fixed_terms", {})}
    t = closing_terms(case, terms, std)
    years = _years(case, t)
    sold = t["volume_per_year"] * years
    old = _units_before(case, t, years) / sold  # sold at the current price
    rate = supplier["interest_rate"]
    pay = 1 - rate * (t["payment_days"] - std["payment_days"]) / 360
    cash_now = 1 + (rate - supplier.get("usual_rate", rate)) * years / 2
    freight = b["freight_eur_per_unit"]
    ppm = supplier.get("ppm", std.get("ppm_commitment") or 0)
    return (
        t["unit_price"] * (1 - old) * pay
        + old * (b.get("current_unit_price") or 0.0) * pay
        + freight[t["incoterm"]]
